translation_updates.summary: Thermodynamics is the branch of physics that examines how heat and work move energy through physical systems, and how that exchange constrains matter and radiation through the related concept of entropy. Four governing laws describe these exchanges in measurable, macroscopic terms, while statistical mechanics supplies a microscopic account of the same behavior. The field took shape in the early nineteenth century out of efforts to improve the efficiency of steam engines, with Sadi Carnot's 1824 analysis of engine efficiency an early landmark; Rudolf Clausius introduced the term entropy in 1865 while working out the second law. The field now comprises several distinct branches — including chemical, equilibrium, non-equilibrium, classical, and statistical thermodynamics — each built on a different model or applied to a different class of system.

In mathematical logic and theoretical computer science, type theory studies formal systems that sort expressions and mathematical objects into types, with each type restricting how an expression may be formed and used, in a way loosely comparable to how a data type constrains values in a programming language. Bertrand Russell worked out the approach between 1902 and 1908 to avoid paradoxes such as the one bearing his name in naive set theory, arriving by 1908 at a hierarchy of types paired with a reducibility axiom, both later formalized in his and Alfred North Whitehead's Principia Mathematica (1910–1913). In the twentieth century the field developed alongside Alonzo Church's lambda calculus and now includes systems such as Per Martin-Löf's intuitionistic type theory, which supports a constructive approach to mathematical foundations, and Thierry Coquand's calculus of constructions, which underlies proof assistants including Rocq (formerly Coq) and Lean.

Franz Brentano (1838–1917) was a German philosopher and psychologist whose 1874 book Psychology from an Empirical Standpoint, regarded as his major work, is credited with bringing the scholastic-era notion of intentionality — the idea that mental acts are directed at objects — back into modern philosophical discussion. He trained and served as a Catholic priest before withdrawing in 1873 over the church's newly declared dogma of papal infallibility, and in 1874 took a full professorship at the University of Vienna. He lost that position in 1880: Austro-Hungarian law barred former priests from marrying, and after he and Ida von Lieben wed abroad the authorities declined to reinstate him, so he taught on as an unsalaried Privatdozent until 1895. His Vienna students included Edmund Husserl, Sigmund Freud, Alexius Meinong, Carl Stumpf, and Kazimierz Twardowski. Husserl, who studied under Brentano before founding the phenomenological movement, carried the concept of intentionality forward along his own, distinct lines rather than co-originating it. Drawing heavily on Aristotle and later scholastic philosophy, Brentano is now often described as anticipating both the phenomenological and analytic traditions in twentieth-century philosophy.

Allen Newell (1927–1992) was an American computer scientist and cognitive psychologist who worked at the RAND Corporation before moving to Carnegie Mellon University. With Herbert A. Simon and programmer Cliff Shaw, he built the Information Processing Language and, in 1956, the Logic Theorist — one of the earliest artificial intelligence programs — followed the next year by the General Problem Solver; his contributions to those programs are credited with helping establish artificial intelligence as a field. Newell and Simon went on to formulate the physical symbol system hypothesis — that intelligent behavior in general amounts to symbol manipulation of the sort their own programs performed — and in 1975 the two shared the ACM Turing Award for their contributions to artificial intelligence and the psychology of human cognition.

Herbert A. Simon (1916–2001) was an American polymath whose contributions spanned computer science, economics, and cognitive psychology; he is best known for the concepts of bounded rationality and satisficing in decision-making. Together with Allen Newell, he built some of the earliest artificial intelligence programs, including the Logic Theory Machine (1956) and the General Problem Solver (1957); that work is often cited as foundational to artificial intelligence and to neighboring fields such as operations research, management science, and cognitive science. Simon and Newell shared the 1975 ACM Turing Award, and in 1978 Simon alone received the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences for his research into decision-making within economic organizations.

verdicts.notes: generator self-flags: The opening sentence restates the same facts as the article's lead (heat/work/energy/entropy/matter/radiation) in different structure and wording; QC should confirm this counts as adequate paraphrase distance rather than a reworded lead. | Citation 4 ('In 1865 he named the concept of entropy') refers back to Clausius by pronoun in the source paragraph — confirm the antecedent is unambiguous when checked against the live page in isolation. | The branch list (chemical, equilibrium, non-equilibrium, classical, statistical) is drawn from five separate section headers in the source rather than a single citable sentence, so no citation names all five together — each branch name individually appears in the article's structure.

sources.quote: In mathematical logic, and theoretical computer science, type theory is the study of formal systems that classify expressions or mathematical objects by their types.
type theory is the study of formal systems that classify expressions or mathematical objects by their types
Between 1902 and 1908, Bertrand Russell proposed various solutions to this problem.

By 1908, Russell arrived at a ramified theory of types together with an axiom of reducibility, both of which appeared in Whitehead and Russell's Principia Mathematica published in 1910, 1912, and 1913.
One influential system is Per Martin-Löf's intuitionistic type theory, which was proposed as a foundation for constructive mathematics.
Another is Thierry Coquand's calculus of constructions, which is used as the foundation by Rocq (previously known as Coq), Lean, and other computer proof assistants.

verdicts.notes: generator self-flags: The opening sentence is structurally close to the source's own definition sentence despite lexical substitution (sort/classify, into/by) — worth a close-read comparison. | Compressed Principia Mathematica's three publication years (1910, 1912, 1913) into the range '1910–1913'; this is a standard shorthand but technically not identical to the source's three-year enumeration. | Did not cite plato.stanford.edu/entries/type-theory/ even though it was in the source set — its content (paradoxes, ramified hierarchy, proof theory) was more technical than needed for a 2–5 sentence summary and the Wikipedia article covered the same ground more concisely. | The phrases naming Martin-Löf's and Coquand's specific systems ('Per Martin-Löf's intuitionistic type theory', 'Thierry Coquand's calculus of constructions') overlap the citation quotes almost word-for-word — these are proper theory names rather than paraphrasable prose, so exact naming seemed preferable to a looser rewrite, but flagging the overlap for QC to judge.

notes: Editorial batch 7 — the public-surface half of session #60 Track B. Earns the en summary + indexable flip for the five nodes held-trigger-nodes-v1 added, keeping the editorial gap at 0.

Regime: separated-context generation (ordered as Opus per decisions (26)/(76) — see the provenance correction below; it actually ran on claude-sonnet-5) grounded in the fetch-corpus captures collected for the Track B QC, then orchestrator machine QC + close-read. Machine: fetch-verify 25/25 PASS pre-patch, 29/29 PASS post-patch, every quote checked against the live page. Close-read: 5/5 = 100% (single-digit batch, the (107) precedent, well above the (34) sampling floor).

★ Close-read caught one factual error, and it was the batch-defining one: the draft said Brentano "from 1874 to 1895 held a professorship at the University of Vienna". SEP says otherwise — he took the full professorship in 1874 but lost it in 1880, because Austro-Hungarian law barred former priests from marrying and the authorities declined to reinstate him after he wed abroad; he taught on as an unsalaried Privatdozent ("a status that allowed him to go on teaching — but did not entitle him to receive a salary or to supervise theses") until 1895. Patched to the accurate chronology with two added SEP citations, then re-verified. Under decision (34) one error returns the batch to full close-read; this batch was already at 100%, so the regime was satisfied without escalation.

Three further patches, all wording drift rather than fact: (1) Newell — the draft rendered the Turing Award citation as "machine intelligence and the science of human cognition"; restored to the sourced "artificial intelligence and the psychology of human cognition". (2) Simon — the Nobel clause "research growing out of that same interest in organizational decision-making" asserted a causal link the source does not; replaced with the sourced subject matter. (3) Both subfield summaries omitted the discipline home entirely; each now opens by naming it, with the defining lead sentence added as a citation.

The generator self-flagged 15 items across the 5 summaries, including the curly-apostrophe character in a SEP quote (correct — it is the literal character) and its own cross-page sourcing of the Simon founding claim (correct, and deliberate: the claim is sourced to the article that names Newell and Simon jointly, per the Track B grain ruling). No self-flag was a false alarm; none of the four patches was something the generator had flagged, which is the argument for keeping close-read at 100% on small batches rather than trusting the flag list.
Living-person check: all five subjects deceased (Brentano 1917, Newell 1992, Simon 2001) or non-person; decision (70) does not engage.

★ PROVENANCE CORRECTION 2026-07-29 (same session, after measurement). This batch was ordered with the Agent tool parameter model:"opus" and its notes originally claimed "Opus subagent" generation per decisions (26)/(76). THAT CLAIM WAS FALSE. Measured directly at session end with two minimal probes that asked a subagent to read its own model ID from its environment: a probe requesting model:"fable" returned claude-sonnet-5, and a probe requesting model:"opus" ALSO returned claude-sonnet-5. The per-call model override was inert for this entire session — env.CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL="sonnet" in ~/.claude/settings.json is read at session start and wins over every per-call value, and removing it mid-session did not take effect. So editorial generation for this batch actually ran on claude-sonnet-5, not Opus. The orchestrator recorded the ORDER-s intent rather than the RUN-s fact, which is precisely the failure the proposal-generator contract already prevents by making the agent self-report proposed_by.model_version from its own environment. Editorial orders carried no such requirement; they now must.

★ Unintended A/B measurement, now the honest reading of this batch. Decision (26) measured editorial summaries at Opus 11/11 vs Sonnet 1/11, and decision (76) recorded editorial-on-Sonnet-5 as an explicitly UNMEASURED A/B candidate not to be adopted blindly. Because the override was inert, session #60-s four editorial batches were that A/B, run accidentally on Sonnet 5. Result as measured this session: batch 7 needed 4 patches including one factual error (Brentano-s Vienna professorship); batches 8, 9 and 10 needed zero substantive corrections, with the only batch-10 edit coming from the generator-s own flag. This is real evidence and it must not be read as an Opus result. It is also not yet a ratified routing change — decision (26)/(76) still stand until a CPO ruling, and n=4 batches from one session with a hardening order template is a weak basis on its own.
